COVERStrands of DNA-like thread coil, loop, and spill upward, evoking the genome’s dynamic three-dimensional architecture within the nucleus of a living cell. This special issue, with papers inScienceandScience Advances, features single-cell and multiomic studies from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund’s 4D Nucleome Program, which examines a fourth dimension of nuclear organization—how this folded structure shapes cell identity, shifts across development and aging, and goes awry in disease. See page364and10.1126/sciadv.aek6870.

Illustration: A. Fisher/Science

ONLINE COVERStrands of DNA-like thread coil, loop, and spill upward, evoking the genome's dynamic three-dimensional architecture within the nucleus of a living cell. This special issue, with papers inScienceandScience Advancesfeatures single-cell and multiomic studies from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund's 4D Nucleome Program, which examines a fourth dimension of nuclear organization—how this folded structure shapes cell identity, shifts across development and aging, and goes awry in disease. Researchers mapped genome architecture across contexts ranging from the aging and Alzheimer's-affected brain to the failing heart and maturing immune cells, alongside new computational tools for reading this architecture in previously understudied tissue.

Credit: A. Fisher/Science

ONLINE COVERA memento to 10 years of exceptional immunology.Science Immunologycelebrates its 10th anniversary this month with aspecial issueon immune memory. Three Reviews explore how multiple layers of immune memory develop and contribute to lifelong immune protection.Divangahi and Kaufmannreview how innate immune memory (or “trained” immunity) is continuously shaped throughout the human lifespan.Turneret al.examine how memory is an actively enforced but adaptable feature of T cells. Finally,Gaya and Good-Jacobsonreview recent research on memory B cell development and function, with a focus on lung-resident memory B cells, which may inform future mucosal vaccination strategies. The special issue also features anEditorialthat reflects on 10 years of exceptional immunology research and commentary published inScience Immunology. This month’s cover illustration depicts an avatar of the immune system playing a memory game, in which previously encountered pathogens are remembered. The scene is framed by an unspooling chromosome, highlighting the critical role that epigenetic reprogramming plays in both innate and adaptive immune memory.

ONLINE COVERLegged Robots. Quadrupedal animals demonstrate remarkable adaptability by coordinating multiple motor skills to navigate a wide range of terrains. In contrast, quadrupedal robots have yet to attain the same level of versatility and adaptability.Kanget al.have now developed a control framework called Action Pretrained Transformer-based Reinforcement Learning for multiskill locomotion of quadrupedal robots at high speed across unstructured terrain. Real-world experiments in urban and forested environments demonstrated the potential to traverse various obstacles including stairs, stepping stones, and gaps. This month’s cover is a photograph of a quadrupedal robot jumping over a fallen tree trunk.

ONLINE COVERThis week,Zhanget al.report that the RNA-editing enzyme dADAR maintains intestinal stem cell quiescence and promotes gut function during aging in fruit flies by inhibiting MAPK signaling. In humans and mice, reductions in colonic ADAR2 were associated with aging and with intestinal regeneration. The image shows a midgut from a young fly in which intestinal stem cells are labeled in green and red and nuclei are stained blue.

ONLINE COVERGut Matters. The cover illustrates the trafficking of regulatory immunoglobulin A (IgA)–producing plasma cells (purple) from the gut mucosa to the bloodstream during treatment with anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies (turquoise) for multiple sclerosis (MS). Anti-CD20 therapy depletes circulating B cells (depicted in blood vessel) and increases the abundance of cytokines (yellow dots) that regulate B cells, such as B cell–activating factor (BAFF) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL).Nezirajet al.investigated longitudinal changes in circulating B cell subpopulations in response to anti-CD20 therapy in patients with MS, finding increases in regulatory mucosal-derived IgA-producing B cells in the blood, a finding that was mirrored in a mouse model. Moreover, the authors observed increased BAFF and APRIL concentrations in plasma, which were associated with certain measures of treatment outcome. These findings suggest that B cell regulation might contribute to the therapeutic effects of anti-CD20 therapy.
